utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you both. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you three as well. Colonel we are continuing and hopefully finishing with your cross-examination, and then I understand there will be a short re-examination and possibly some questions from the bench. So let's start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Selak and welcome back to your last day here, at least this trip. I need you to have the war diary again, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor has it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going very close to the end of that document, sir. The page is 4736. 250 -- 260 in English. 4736.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll find an entry, I believe, that reads as follows: "At 1100 hours, a group of military judges and Prosecutors arrived because of a large number of cases pending trial. The Court was ordered to organise round the clock work and to update cases as soon as possible. The misdemeanors magistrate will also work on a 24-hour basis." Based on your military experience, would you have any idea what this backlog of cases was? What kind of cases it was that these judges and Prosecutors were coming there to work around the clock trying to deal with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it was a large number of deserters that were being tried, deserters from the units and failure to respond to the call-up and mobilisation call, to report to the military units, and other infringements against military provisions and laws, which all military personnel come under, and citizens employed, civilians employed in military units as well are subject to those laws and provisions. It is not the civil courts that are in charge of persons of that kind but the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it would also be, I suppose, fair to assume that some of these cases might also have had to deal with these problems of looting that have been mentioned throughout here and that General Talic seemed to be so concerned about. Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I would like it to be so, because that would have prevented looting and plunder, yes, and this would have made the authority of the unit greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to do this as quickly as I can. There are two places in this war diary, sir, one is -- it's page 68 in the English edition, if you want to look at it, it's 4566. I don't think you need to but you can if you want. And then the other place is at page 101 in the English, and that would be, for you, 4597. Both of those places, the diary speaks of businessmen from Banja Luka arriving for visits to the command. The first one just says that, businessmen [Realtime transcript read in error "American"] from Banja Luka arrived for a visit. The second entry -- and that was 11 July. The second entry, 20 July, "A group of private businessmen from Banja Luka arrived today and brought us various radio sets as a gift." What would be the purpose for businessmen coming to the forward command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Businessmen came to the forward command because it was certainly in their interests for the army to perform the tasks intended for it. And so both materially and financially, they assisted it. There were donors who supplied money, who gave money contributions to assist the army and others would give material goods in this case various appliances, equipment and so on. I know for a fact that businessmen came to visit very frequently both from private firms and socially owned and social organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know what it -- do you have any idea what it would mean that they brought various radio sets as a gift? A gift to who? What would that all be about? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio receivers. They are not radio stations. They were radio receivers for the work -- battery operated, they were, these radio sets so that the officers and soldiers in the trenches up at the front could, say, hear the news over the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Colonel, I notice that the last entry, the one page -- relating to 20 August, refers to a date when you had already left the army. How do you know these things? How do you know what kind of radios were brought over by the businessmen from Banja Luka? And incidentally for the record, as far as the first entry is concerned, the transcript refers to American businessmen from Banja Luka, which is incorrect. You never mentioned American businessmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He never did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 3 line 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the information media, let me explain, on television, in the press, radio Banja Luka, there were cases broadcast of this type, and while I was an active duty officer, they would come to my own units, giving gifts of other products, not only technical goods but other things, even clothing and gloves, things of that kind, too so that's how I know. And I heard it over television and the radio and the other information media. It was quite customary even before, not only during the war. This was done in peacetime too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, the next place I want to direct you to is page 4550. It's page 51 English, and --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Give me a moment to find it. 4550, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually, I think it's 4549 -- no it's 4550. I'm right the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are referring to the entry of the 6th July, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you find it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right at the very end of that day's entry, you'll see an entry, "The General left for Banja Luka to attend a service marking the death of Colonel Milan Stevilovic and the others." The question I want to ask you about that is: Was it to your knowledge customary, required, for any time the general left the area that it be entered in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not customary, because that was his professional duty. He had to attend commemorative sessions of this kind and other meetings, but the officer on duty saw fit to record that. And the person on duty knew where the commander was going, so he didn't actually have to enter all those details into the logbook but it's up to the duty officer and the team on duty, in fact, to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there is no requirement that the duty officer account for General Talic leaving the command for a period of time? That doesn't have to be in the logbook? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that when the corps commander or unit commander, whichever, leaves his office, well people aren't going to record where he's gone every time. He just tells his deputy orally or the team on duty where he's going so that he can be reached in an emergency. Now, if he goes further away from the area of responsibility or he goes up to the front to visit some operative groups, then he would have to write in the time he left and where he left for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that we are understanding each other. What I'm not asking you is whether the purpose of his trip needs to be recorded. What I'm asking you is if it's required that some mention be put in the logbook that General Talic has left for Banja Luka, for instance. Or can he just go without that ever showing up in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had to be recorded in the logbook. Information of that kind had to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can also take the form of an official note written by the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I have you look at, then, let's do this as quickly as I can, 4590? That would be page 92 English. I'll tell you it simply says: "At 1000 hours General Talic left for a meeting in Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment please. I have the page but I haven't found at 1000 hours, that passage. Yes, I see it I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you if you go to 4606 --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 22 July, you see General Talic left for a meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you go to page 4655, the very last entry on that page for 6 August, 164 English?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It not only records that he went to Banja Luka but says why, "General Talic left for Banja Luka to attend a meeting at which all units of the 1st Krajina Corps were given clear instructions for further operations in the Krajina section of the front." Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in this case, they also recorded the purpose, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at 4674, right at the very beginning, at 0800 hours, "General Talic left for Banja Luka and the forward command post at Kula Mrkonjic Grad, to meet the President of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Radovan Karadzic for talks on the situation on the front and the organisation of the Serbian army." So he had gone there to have a meeting basically with the Commander-in-Chief, had he not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the last one, sir, look at page 4707, part way through the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- entry for 21 August, "General Talic stayed in Banja Luka for a meeting with the commanders of brigades and the presidents of municipalities from the area covered by the 1st Krajina Corps. They discussed the situation on the front and functioning of authority." Now, I will tell you that I have not been able to find any other entries in this war diary about General Talic leaving and going to Banja Luka except the six that we have just talked about. And among the six that we have just talked about, none of those indicated that he was going to Banja Luka to meet with Mr. Brdjanin or with the President of the ARK Crisis Staff or anything of that nature, do they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, but he did have his representatives or rather his assistants. He had an assistant for moral guidance and legal affairs, Colonel Vukelic, head of security, Colonel Stevo Bogojevic and Colonel Vujnovic - what was his first name - Gojko Vujnovic, and they attended those meetings or rather they could attend those meetings on his behalf. And Colonel Marcetic the head, the Chief of Staff. So General Talic didn't always have to be present but he was always informed by his subordinates and they would attend these sessions both in the municipality and of the Regional Crisis Staff on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Finally we are finished with the war diary, no more questions about that. I want you to take -- I want to ask you this question first, see if you recall this. During my cross-examination of you two or three days ago, we were talking about the organisation of Muslims in Kozarac and the arming of Muslims in Kozarac and I think where we finally got was you agreed that certainly some of the Muslim people in that area would have had weapons, hunting weapons and other kinds of weapons but I think you rather emphatically told us that there was no organised TO units, Muslim TO units, operating in that area. Did I fairly characterise what you told us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you give a page reference for that on the LiveNote?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can't, I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last few days he's been forgetting that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say that a number -- a certain number of citizens had hunting weapons, with the legal permits, but I believe that another part of the population did not have permits for the weapons that they could procure, but what I was saying was that there was no military organisation on the part of the Muslims, the Bosniaks. Military formations. I don't know about the weapons. I don't know how many people did have weapons. But I'm sure that a lot of them did, because those were the kinds of times they were. People were afraid for their lives and afraid for the lives of their families and in that kind of situation I'm sure I would buy a weapon too to protect myself and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say there was no military organisation, what you're saying there was no organised or mobilised Muslim TO units there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is this: That in the local communities, people set up barricades in order to control the passage of certain vehicles and they organised themselves --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is simple. Were there organised or mobilised TO units in Kozarac? That's all I want to know from you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at DB127? Now, there are two things I'd like you to pay attention to with regard to this document. One is that it's entitled, "List of mobilisation," and the second is that each page refers to Stab, TO Kozarac. And what you should find and take your time and look through it, is a list of members of the TO Kozarac and the weapons which they possessed, and when you've read it --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I can see the signatures and it says, "Hunting rifle, pistol, 7.65, et cetera." Underneath that the people who don't have any. And of the 33, I see that only three or four men were armed, in fact, out of the 33 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you keep going, you're going to find that there were quite a few weapons and you're going to find that several of them were sort of classic military weapons.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page A 12 of the 28 persons there, not a single one, nor does it say -- of the 49 people, there is a hunting rifle, it says here pistol, 7.62, one has a M-48 rifle and that's all. All I can see of all these 49 people mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is a PAP? Can you tell me what a PAP?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A semi-automatic rifle. Where did you see the PAP?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at A/1/13, entry number 27, you'll see that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 27, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dedo Karabasic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please. I'm not looking at the same thing, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the upper right-hand corner, you should see an A/1/13.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 3/4 -- yes, just a moment. I don't seem to be on the same page. 12? That's fine. Under 27, yes, it says here semi-automatic rifle, personal weapon for Dedo Karabasic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go you go up to number 17 can you tell us what a automasko licno oruzje is or whatever? I can't read that. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic personal weapon. Well it could be an automatic gun, a pistol -- it could be a pistol or a rifle. A personal weapon. It doesn't say clearly what it is, but it is a weapon, a personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think a M-48 is kind of an older model military weapon, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Manufactured in 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's clear from these that someone was making a serious effort to list all the people and the weapons that they had with regard to this stab TO Kozarac or TO, BiH, Kozarac, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this could be expected. People were not going to voluntarily offer their heads, but were going to try to protect their lives. From what you can see, one can conclude that this is a minimum of what a unit of the Territorial Defence should normally have. This is the strictest minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look at --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2 per cent of the people were armed here, according to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at page A/1/82, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A/1/82? Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Number 77 on that list, I can't -- I don't know what that means, after the entry. I don't know whether that says zolja or what that says, that looks like it says two bomb?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "zolja - two hand grenades," and then this other thing I'm not sure, but that's what it says. All these weapons could be normally obtained on the black market, that is on the local market. So this really does not reflect anything. I mean, all this in case of a normal operative army, operative military, these are just toys.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's awfully different from what you told us was absolutely no organised TO units in Kozarac, isn't it? There clearly was organised TO units in Kozarac. They signed up, they declared their weapons, the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is just a list of people and weapons that they possess. This is not a military formation, because in a military formation, the strength of the unit would be regulated, including the company, platoons, and so on and so forth, including also who the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. commander officer was and the Chief of Staff. Here I only see a list of people who could have been organised if -- if I'd been there, I would have organised them. Unfortunately, they were not organised themselves and this is why the genocide took place, because they had no one to defend them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now what I want you to do is go to page A/1/93.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I think what you see on those pages there is a formal or formal mobilisation orders for the TO Kozarac, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here, "General mobilisation call, local community Kozarac," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished with that document, sir. I'm now going to ask you to again take out your notebook, we will try to get through some things in there very quickly that I want to talk to you about, and then we'll be finished.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. First place we are going is 26 December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under number 2, commander's report, there is a -- it says VBS, and then in our translation, there is some question about what that is. The translator thinks it's military hospital Sarajevo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite right. The Sarajevo military hospital, and now we see the problems of the specialists, the problems with the personal income, which at the time was 15.000. Here we also see that they lacked some basic medicines such as the kofan and other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I was interested in with regard to this, just to bring your attention to, the shortage of basic medical supplies, was that a continuing problem during this period of time or not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a continuing problem at the time, but it -- we also -- they also had a problem with electricity cuts, power shortages, and the fact that they did not have enough generators -- well, actually no, they did have electricity on the 26th of December, 1991, but they were already lacking medicine. The problem with energy would arise only later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Outside, going outside Sarajevo now, into the -- your area of responsibility, was there a problem there with shortage of basic medical supplies, during primarily early 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was. We managed to get via Belgrade, that is from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, something; the corridor had been established in the meantime. But it is true that medicines for treating combatants and the civilian population in general were lacking in the Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And especially during that period of time that the corridor was closed and supplies couldn't come from Belgrade, it became a rather critical problem, did it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It became a problem for all, for the military and civilian authorities in this area, and I'm sure that there were consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look, if you will, please, now, just a little further down, there is a -- it's "see chief of army housing institution." There is an entry there that says: "Programme for tenants to buy out their apartments, paper work prepared." Can you explain to us what that was about.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what page are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the same date, 26 December, just a little further down from where we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a "see chief of army housing institution," and then it talks about a programme for tenants to buy out their apartments, paper work prepared?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I see. The programme to buy out the apartments, that such a programme was prepared, you mean. What is referred to is the action of buying out the apartments that were property of the housing fund, and that could be bought by the active duty servicemen and other employees of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So these -- correct me if I'm wrong -- these were apartment that is were previously owned by the army, basically, and then the army decided to allow the active duty servicemen to purchase those apartments if they wished to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Active duty officers. Conscripts who were doing their military service did not have such right. Only officers and civilians employed with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know when that programme was initiated? Was it around this time in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is when it started, and I think it lasted until the 15th of February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Go just a little further now to number 5, Colonel Milicevic on mobilisation. There is an entry that says "The general manpower level in the first military district at 60 per cent." Does that mean that the units are only overall at 60 per cent of authorised strength?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, the strength was also -- only 60 per cent of the 1st military district. That is to say a mobilisation had been proclaimed and a number of people did not respond. However, in respect of certain units, the mobilisation was declared null and void because combat operations were not taking place in the entire area of responsibility of the 1st military district, and that is why the mobilisation was declared null and void, because there were other units who were in charge of the rest of the Bosnian Krajina and it was only logical that not all units should be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who had the power to declare a mobilisation null and void? Who could do that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say invalid. The commander of the 1st military district could in respect of the units on the territory of the Republic of Serbia choose not to declare such a mobilisation. It is his right to decide which of his units are going to be mobilised on the basis of his assessment of the situation and what units he needed. The general mobilisation in the entire area of the former Yugoslavia could only be declared by the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But the question, and think we have a translation problem, you had told us that the mobilisation was declared -- for parts of the area, was declared null and void. I did not say "invalid." I said "null and void," which I think is what you said. My question is: Who has the power to declare a mobilisation null and void?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who has that power? Who can do that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st military district, in respect of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go now to -- on the same date to paragraph 8, General Vidovic. "General Vidovic reports that military courts convicted 232 persons." Would you have any idea what kind of offences these were, the people were being convicted for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In respect of the 1st military district, like I said, it covered a very large area from Novi Sad all way to the southern Serbia including Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Mostar. It was a huge area and I really -- I didn't know. I wasn't interested in that. I just made a note in my notebook. I Just wrote down this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you go now to 7 January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Here I have the 6th. Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right before 7 January, do you have a page in your notebook that has a list of a bunch of page numbers, or is this something that's just in our translation? It says page 95, page 120, 121, 132 through 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's at page 24, Your Honours, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have that right before the January 7 entry? Just a list of page numbers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On page 29 of my diary, before the 7th of January, I have a conversation with a commander of the 2nd military warehouse, and I have enumerated the items and there are seven numbers, seven items on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you not being correct. Look, please, at page 01036889, and at the back of it, 01036890. These are the numbers or the entry that Mr. Ackerman is referring you to, to confirm whether they exist or not in your original diary and notebook, and they do exist because I have them here in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please. You can have a look at my notebook. I don't have that in my notebook. I don't know what we are talking about. Here. Have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It must be there. I don't think anyone invented it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't that he was denying the mistakes. The point I'm trying to make it wasn't that he was denying it was there, whatever Your Honour is looking at, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the page that you indicated, sir, no, I didn't say anything in respect of other pages. Please refer me to the exact page and we will solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm doing the best I can but I can't find it either, so I'm not surprised that you can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, as I can see it, it's somewhere between the 3rd January 1992 entry and the 8 January 1992 entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to, I can have a look at the English version and try to help. It will maybe remind me of the equivalent page in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we will do, Colonel, very simply put -- Usher, please come here. Give this to the witness. Show him this page and the back of it, and then he will find it in his original for sure because I'm pretty sure this is not something which is made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you also show this him. This is what the English version that I have looks like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is my handwriting. Whether this is from the same notebook, I don't know. Let me just have a look. These should be the same pages as the ones in the notebook. I think I wrote this as my personal notes of important things with respect of this war diary. The page number is 95. Let me have a look, please. Yes. Once again, this is my handwriting but I don't have it in my notebook. I don't know where it can be found, but it is my handwriting. The last entry, page 64, makes mention of the financing of the VRS from -- by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, at the situation as of the 20th of May. Yes, I can only confirm that this is my handwriting but I still don't have it in my notebook and these are the page numbers of my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it likely a document you prepared for the Office of the Prosecutor to direct them to the parts of your notebook that you thought important?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Here is a piece of paper where I made note of the important things, the things that I consider to be significant from this notebook. I have prepared them for this occasion as well, in order not to wander too much. If you ask me so that I can quote the correct information, in order not to waste time. Only for that reason. You can check the number of the diary page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing at this point to let it all remain a mystery but I do -- I would like my piece of paper back. We had made it to 7 January then, and the only thing I wanted to call your attention to on that page --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only thing I want to draw your attention to is under quartermaster service, they mention a shortage of sugar. Was that a continuing problem or was that just at that particular time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. This was reported by the chief quartermaster officer, that there was a shortage of sugar, and that we would have to borrow it from work organisations. What we are talking about here is the sugar needed for the units in the area of responsibility of the logistical base. He said that we should go ahead with the borrowing and that we would return them -- the commodity later on because the problem needed to be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Go now to 8 January, please, the next day, under political and moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says under 30 per cent of men present in the units, that means that more than 70 per cent aren't? Is this because of desertion? Or what is this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. See here, an approval was issued that the units who do not need to have a reserve component because they are not taking part in combat operations, if they are able to perform their tasks with the peace time force, that they can return the surplus of their human resources to the enterprises. This is what we are talking about here. I personally did not have any problems with the manpower, and I gave my consent to the commander. I told the commander of -- commanders of my subordinate units that they should return these people if they did not need them to the economy, to various businesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if we go to the next day, just the very next day, 9 January, under the heading, "Reporting," for instance the 2nd ammunition depot commander reports a large number of unauthorised absences, unauthorised departure by conscripts is probable and expected, that people are stealing weapons from you," doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat? Because what I have -- oh, reporting for the 9th. And you're referring to the next page? The page after that? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "2nd ammunition depot commander reports that there are a large number of unauthorised absences," in fact it's more than that. "There are shootouts around the town at guard posts, ten conscripts went AWOL from their unit, not coming back, can't afford experimenting with the military organisation, a large number of unauthorised absences, unauthorised departure by conscripts probable and expected, and stealing of weapons." Those are things he reports, right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Major Obrad Nikic from the ammunition depot in Mrkonjic Grad where the command of the 30th Partisan Division of the Colonel, now general, Galic was located. That was his command post and it is true that they had problems. However, the unit managed to carry out all of their assignments. They were burdened with some other problems, which this person is indicating here, but the issue was finally resolved with Colonel Galic at the time, who was based in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the question that -- the thing that baffles me about this and- that maybe you can help me with is this: This is a military installation. It's an ammunition depot. How is it that they are not able to provide sufficient security to keep people from stealing weapons? How can that be?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Weapons were arriving on a daily basis by trucks, but they also left in trucks, to the units of the corps, and we were informed of this problem. However, the human factor, or rather the mobilisation, resulted in the fact that there was a large number of dissatisfied people who were afraid for their safety and they simply fled. We are talking about ten conscripts, people who had been mobilised, who had left the unit on their own, and the problem was discussed, but there were many units that were faced with this kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... This is probably related to this unauthorised departure by conscripts and as they unauthorisedly departed they took weapons with them, thereby stealing them? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They weren't stealing them. They were close by and so, from Mrkonjic and the neighbouring villages, from the Mrkonjic municipality, the commander of their company and platoon allowed them to take weapons because the people were afraid. This was contrary to military provisions and laws, but unfortunately that's what happened. So they didn't actually agree to them taking the weapons home, but I had a lot of problems in that warehouse for -- because of other matters. I don't want to focus on that now in this courtroom, but perhaps I could make a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, in the entry, the third entry from the bottom, under one, reporting, number 1, second ammunition depot commander, you do have stealing of weapons. So what is being referred to or meant by that entry? If it's not what you have been mentioning, what kind of stealing of weapons is being referred to? Stealing of weapons from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The weapons were stolen from the units themselves. There were cases when the duty officer of the unit, the unit in a company, a soldier would be on duty and would go to sleep while on duty. And people would take advantage of this, seize the weapons, and carry them off home. So things like that did happen. I never said they didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, on the next page, it's the entry about the third fuel depot.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "130 conscripts would like to volunteer after the mobilisation announcement." What does that mean? They are already Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. conscripts. What are they volunteering for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this is about is that some of these soldiers were released and left to go home. The commander of the warehouse discharged the soldiers, the surplus soldiers, the ones he didn't need, and they were allowed to go home. However, people still came in because they would be given money, and so probably they didn't have enough money and then volunteered. They wanted to be called up into the units first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Go now to number 16, in this same list where we were just at number 3. Just keep going until you get to number 16 which talks about the quartermaster service, and the quartermaster service --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 5? Not 16. I apologise but I think it's number 5, the quartermaster service. We talked about number 3, 4 were the reserve parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Keep going.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go to 16, it's quartermaster service. You're looking at quartermaster stores.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "some manufacturers cancelling orders." These would be orders the army had given to these manufacturers who are now cancelling them and not supplying what the army had asked for? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And were they doing that because of this shortage problem we've been discussing, the inability to get the raw materials necessary to fulfil these -- those orders?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was so. I didn't say which goods they were, which materials, but I do believe that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just out of curiosity, there is throughout your notebook on occasion, you refer to one combat set of ammunition. Could you tell us what one combat set of ammunition consists of?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One combat set of ammunition is a pistol, six bullets, for an automatic rifle or rather the M-48, 7, 9 millimetres, that would be five bullets and so on. For a tank, for example, let's take the T-55 tank, 35 grenades. So every type of weapon would have a combat set of ammunition that would be issued for it. And so this is a mathematical calculation. When the commander plans an operation of any kind, he tells the units what part of the combat set they can use, artillery ammunition and so on, infantry ammunition and so on. So these are calculations and this was essential to have the necessary supplies. It was also essential because it stipulated how much ammunition each person could have with him so as not to weigh down the soldiers in combat, and these supplies were filled by the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you. If you go to January 14th, the last entry on January 14th, you indicate that you were informed that a Golf car was missing from the headquarters administration staff with an automatic rifle and one combat set of ammunition. So that would mean an automatic rifle and, like, six rounds or something. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I've found the 14th of January but -- yes. Here it is. The last one. Just a moment, please. Security, specifications, I don't know what this is. I was informed at exactly 1230 hours. Probably the chief of security because I see that underneath that, point 11, refers to the chief of security and I don't know what was undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm really trying to move a little more rapidly. And the only thing I'm interested in here is: With that automatic rifle, one combat set of ammunition would have been how many rounds?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For an automatic rifle that would be eight -- 16 bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told us --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two rounds of eight bullets each, 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us a few minutes ago when we were talking about mobilisation, and this was referring to JNA times, that it was only the -- I think you said the president of the republic that could order a full -- the president of SFRY, that could order a full Yugoslav JNA mobilisation. Is that what you said? I don't want to misquote you. Just tell me if that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said in peacetime. If the assembly cannot meet, the assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, then what happens is that on its behalf, the decisions are made by the Presidency on all issues including that of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when the -- when the VRS was formed, and the rules and regulations that had previously dictated operations within JNA were adopted, then it would have been the Presidency of Republika Srpska that would have been able to declare public mobilisation in the absence of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that the constitution of the Serb Republic of -- actually, I haven't read the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but I think this was done in the name of the assembly and the president of the republic and the Supreme Commander can make decisions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What about the Ministry of National Defence? Would the Ministry of National Defence actually be the organ that would announce and organise that mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence is at the head of the units, and if it has being given authorisation from the competent authorities, that is to say the assembly or the Supreme Commander, rather the President, then it would have to conduct preparations, and to proclaim a mobilisation, I don't think it can do so on its own bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at, and I just kind of want to get your take on P137, please. 137. Let me see what you have there. That doesn't look right to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ackerman, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If necessary, I can live without that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 371. Let's try that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You have a document signed by a person named Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic, and I think you and I talked about him briefly last week, did we not, or earlier this week?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what this purports to be, among other things, is a decision ordering the general public mobilisation on the whole territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I take it that somebody in the position of Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Sajic could not, on his own, declare a mobilisation, but that that authority had to come from the highest levels of government, and here it says the Ministry of National Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is the source, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your notebook. I want you to look under 16 January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if you go, there is an introduction under that there is a 1 and a 2, and if you keep going, then you'll get to another area, where there is also a 1 and a 2. It's that second 2 that I'm interested in, that starts with large consumption of small arms ammunition.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Underneath that there is a paragraph that -- it's not -- it's not well translated, maybe, but here is what it seems to say. "The fact that a state of war has not been declared reflects negatively on logistical support because of the difficulties involved in using the MR, material reserves, of the territory and the SRR, strategic stockpiles, including preventing their use and attempts to hide or perhaps conceal them and obstructing the supply lines." Tell me -- tell us what that all means.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, if you would, or rather I'm looking at this reference to ammunitions in two portions, in two sections. So I'm not sure I can find it. I'm reading this here. "Due to the enormous usage of ammunition."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not where we are. It says, "The fact that a state of war has not been declared." It's under number 2, it's the second number 2. Number 1 is "fuel given to business organisations." Number 2 is "large consumption of small arms ammunition." And then you just go down a couple of paragraphs and you see, "The fact that a state of war has not been declared." It's fairly early on 16 January?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, 54, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mentions --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is that about? What are these material reserves and strategic stockpiles, and how do they relate to whether or not a state of war has been declared?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was large consumption of both ammunition and fuel by the units here, and this is an analysis of the logistics supplies in my own command. The problems were put forward, and we see 80.000 bullets are mentioned here which is what one brigade requires for a 7.65 millimetre pistol. This is a criminal act, because where can a brigade in combat use 80.000 bullets? I ask you. And so the corps commander was supplied with this information. We focused on those figures because they would not have the ammunition they needed when they most required it. So that's why we went to Gornji Milanovac and Skoplje and Tetovo and other towns Serbia to bring in both fuel and ammunition and the other things that were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm really trying to finish and the question I asked you was what -- it's the next paragraph down where we are talking about the fact that a state of war has not been declared. You see that paragraph? "The fact that a state of war has not been declared?"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The fact a state of war has not been declared creates problems to the army, because declaration of a state of war then the units, if that is done, then the units can ask companies to supply them with the necessary material once a state of war has been declared. In peacetime, they have to be contracts signed and agreed upon for several years, but in wartime, the army disposes of human and material potential in its area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These are -- this is materiel that is basically stockpiled, reserves, strategic reserves and material reserves that can only be tapped if there is a declaration of war? I think that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But even then, the material reserves of the territory are given on the basis of a percentage. Let me give you an example. Federal fuel reserves in 1992, in Prijedor, the army was allowed to use a part of those reserves and the autonomous region was allowed to use the other portion, the Energopetrol company and some other companies were given 60 per cent of those republican -- I beg your pardon, I meant republican reserves and federal reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go, please, to 4 February, 1992.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under quartermaster service, it says this: "There is no equipment for military conscripts. There are 1.000 sets with items missing. Requests filed, no response. Factories do not have production material. Stocar has no meat, bread," and then next entry under that, veterinary service, "shortage of meat." It looks like there are quite a few shortages going on on February 4, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the market had undergone upsets already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what is Stocar?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stocar was a company in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that a company that ordinarily supplied meat but because of the supply disruptions was not able to do so? Is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons. The other was that the civilian authorities had to ensure necessary supplies for the population. So there were shortages both for the population at large and the army, and we had to solve this problem as best we could, and we did so in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go now to 7 February, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it written down twice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 7 February --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a meeting with unit commanders and the base command where a functioning of the military organisation. That's the 7 February I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military organisations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go down through there, you'll finally -- there will be a number at the top there is numbers 1, 2 and 3, then you go along and you'll finally get to where there is a second number 2, it says, "Military conscripts refusing guard duty."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is the first warehouse. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How could it be in a military organisation that a conscript could refuse to carry out an order? What kind of a military organisation is that where they say, "No, we are not going to do that"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What this is about is the first ammunitions warehouse in my base in Banja Luka. The commander of the warehouse was Lieutenant Colonel Aljosa Mujagic. And people were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I really don't want to spend the rest of the day asking you questions. If you'll answer the one I ask you, we can finish; if you won't, we won't finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Colonel Selak said -- Your Honour, I'm sorry, I didn't understand what all that is meant to mean. What is a question like: How could a military organisation -- what kind of a military organisation is that? What is the officer supposed to say to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's obviously asking for an explanation. How come that in an army, at this particular time in its history, with all the problems that there were, it seems that military conscripts were refusing guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't -- what is the actual -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. What is that actual question that Colonel Selak is being asked to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, he's being asked to explain how come this was possible within an organised army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Your Honour thinks that that is a question that can be answered, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it. He's showing surprise that this could happen at all, but perhaps Colonel Selak has the explanation ready for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an answer. The warehouse is situated on the outskirts of Banja Luka. The citizens had quite a lot of weapons, and there was a lot of shootings, sporadic shooting around the warehouse and in the woods, and people were afraid to do guard duty. It's all human, and we had to work with human beings to explain to them what was going on and to ensure their safety. They are all children, youngsters, of 18 years, 20 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go down now to just a little ways, number 3, quartermaster battalion where they say they are -- somebody is powerless to stop conscripts from running away home. See that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's beginning to look like an army with little or no discipline?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's also true. The battalion was in town. It was a quartermaster battalion with the bakery detachments and kitchens and so on. People fled to town. I called the commander for a talk. You have this later on in the diary. I invited him for an official meeting, and we drew his attention to that, that he had to ensure the control and functioning of the military organisations he was Major Ivica Malic who had to leave the unit later on and he went to Belgrade when he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to 26 February, 1992, and just look briefly, if we can, a little more about this morale problem. And try to help me work through this?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we just start with the first ammunition depot, "Conditions in quarters, morale on the decline, the evenings men running away home, mass absence in the evenings, food quality mediocre, second ammunition depot status much morale exhausted, lack of enthusiasm, quality of food, no cooks. Second ammunition depot section," that's a little ways further along, "a few undisciplined soldiers creating disorder in the whole section. The third fuel depot, grumbling, men tired of guard duty. Fourth spare parts depot, status of morale, too much strain overworked, security and self protection stagnating, firearm shootouts in the neighbourhood. Quartermaster store, 23 men not back from leave, dissatisfaction with pay and grumbling. Quartermaster battalion, status of morale, dissatisfaction, going AWOL into town." And that's enough of that but there seems to be quite a lot of dissatisfaction in discipline, things of that nature, going on at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The economic state was reflected on moral discipline and insecurity that families felt. People were dissatisfied. There was general chaos. That's all true. And this is after the reporting of subordinate commanders to me that I focused on these critical problems for us to take steps to solve them. But yes, it's true that's what the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we go now to 1 March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think we go for the break instead, Mr. Ackerman. 15 minutes, thank you. In the meantime, just to keep you informed, next witness, in case we opt for, not for the closed session but for voice distortion, whatever, I'm instructing the technicians so that during this break and the next, they will make the necessary technical arrangements for that to be possible should we decide later on to resort to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just not sure whether the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next witness, you had --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just not sure where the next witness is at the moment, and there has to be testing done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know. They will start preparing the microphones and everything and they will do the testing in the second break. That was the idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, we are making progress here. Let's go to 1 March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was told by the technical people, Your Honour, that I'm doing this a little too fast so I'm going to have to slow down just a tad so everybody could keep up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was actually going to ask you to go faster.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 96, 97, I cannot find the 1st of March. I wonder whether the page numbers are correct. No. I don't have the 1st of March in my notebook. Give me just a moment, please. Yes, I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first entry, sir, reads, "At 1400 hours, Lieutenant Darko Savic reported that all roads leading to and from the second ammunition depot section had been blocked." Do you know what that's about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The second ammunition depot section in Donji Vakuf, the commander, Lieutenant Savic, reported that the roads were blocked at 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Blocked by whom? And why?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donji Vakuf is a junction of roads towards Bugojno, Travnik, and Jajce. In the military sense, the authority lay with Colonel Galic; one of his brigades was there. I assume that it was the local communities that carried out the blockade of the roads. However, shortly after that, the problem was resolved and the depot was able to function normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "local communities," you mean local civilian authorities, blockaded the roads leading to and from the second ammunition depot?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is at least my assumption. I didn't note down the details because the problem was quickly resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me take you, please, to 13 April, 1992. This is another entry dealing with Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 132, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 15th? I found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right before an entry that reads, "President of the Bugojno municipal assembly," right before that, there is an entry that starts with, "80 per cent." Let me know when you find that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It says, "80 per cent of Serbs have moved their families out of the area, and about 5 per cent Muslims."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation as to why it was such a high percentage of Serb families that left and such a low percentage of Muslim families?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, the President of the Donji Vakuf municipal assembly, Mr. Terzic is reporting on the problems in Donji Vakuf. He provided this piece of information. I personally was surprised, because after that, the bridge in Donji Vakuf was destroyed by the military, which was there on the 1st of May, 1992. They blew up the bridge to prevent communication with Bugojno. Following that, as you will see later, the Serbian Municipality of Donji Vakuf was proclaimed. We discussed it two days ago. So this information is not correct. Ethnic composition of the population in Donji Vakuf, as far as Serbs and Muslims, that is Bosniaks, are concerned, was such that there were only 1 or 2 per cent Muslims more than Serbs, and there was a total of 4 per cent of Croats living in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you go to 15 April, 1992 now, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll find an entry that says, "Stamenkovic"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just go up a little ways from there, about oh, five or six lines on this issue of discipline -- well, actually there are three entries under Malic regarding discipline. "Lack of discipline in quartermaster battalion units, going AWOL to go home particularly in the baker's company." And then this entry, "company commanders have to beg their men to carry out tasks." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you find it a little bizarre that a company commander has to beg someone to do something rather than order them to do that and expect it to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to 16 April? And there is one 16 April entry that says "Jajce," and then after that, there is another one that says "Meeting".

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look down through the one that says meeting, you'll come to an underlined section called "chief of patrolling sector." When you find, "Chief of patrolling sector," let me know.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chief of communication -- road sector". Do you see letters RH written just above it? Is that the entry you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The entry right above it is a paragraph that starts, "The number of people attended a course in Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you start from the front of that meeting 16 April, you see "a shot was fired from Colonel Galic's escorts," go down further you see, "afraid of the military police." And then right after that, "A number of people attended"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "A number of people attended a course in Zagreb." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see "from the escort of Colonel Galic a bullet was shot during the meeting," and then it goes down, decision by Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I see. A number of people attended a course in Zagreb, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the course was interrupted and there was a refusal to sign a pledge of allegiance to the Republic of Croatia, they came home." Now, who were these people that attended that course, do you know?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The course in question was intended for police officers. It was interrupted and the people who attended it went back home. No other comments, because I didn't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Police officers from Jajce apparently went to this course in Zagreb and the authorities of the Republic of Croatia demanded that they sign a pledge of allegiance to Croatia." Is that your understanding of what happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go, please, to the entry for 5 May.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we touched on this very briefly the other day. Diagonally across that page, there is a rather colourful entry that someone else put there and my question to you about it is: What was that all about? Why was that put there? It looks like somebody was frustrated with you not giving them the supplies that they felt like they needed. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know what this is about. To my left was a colonel from a brigade. Weapons were required. This is all about weapons. A request therefore was made for weapons, and I insisted on the appropriate legal procedure to be applied. The mobilisation -- and then once the appropriate conditions were met, I was willing to issue the weapons. And then he wrote down these words in a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So he was expressing his frustration at being required to follow the regulations? Is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted to speed up the procedure. I didn't have the right -- I mean I did not have an authorisation to issue ammunition and weapons for those units that had not been mobilised, who did not have right to such weapons. The units in question were the units from the left bank of the Sana River, and this Lieutenant Colonel was from one of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you go to 18 May now, please? And we've discussed this again before.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... day that the JNA became the VRS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the item A, under 5th Corps commander, reads, "Information from meeting of the Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your testimony earlier, you concluded that meant that General Talic had attended that meeting, but it doesn't say anywhere that he attended it, just that he is passing along information from it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he's talking about here are the tasks following a Crisis Staff meeting. I'm not claiming that he attended the meeting but it is my assumption because the meeting in question, the session in question, was a very important one, and I see no reason why he wouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, General Talic was in Gradiska at this time, wasn't he? In this period of time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His office was in Gradiska. However, his area of responsibility and his rear command post was in Banja Luka, so he occasionally went to Banja Luka. As far as he's concerned, this was a normal travel, normal form of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question that I really wanted to ask. Thank you. Go to 22 May, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you go back from there to the last entry on 21 May, it says, "Talic," and it says that he extends his welcome to Mr. Cyrus [phoen] and his support regardless of ethnic background. Do you know who Mr. Cyrus was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cyrus Shakaline [phoen] was a representative of the International Red Cross on behalf of the UN high commissioner for refugees. I too was present on that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Go to 29 May, 1992, then, would you, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After the reporting section, the last one being E, fourth spare parts depot, there is an entry called "duties for commanders."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who is it that would have been assigning those duties? Who does this come from? Does this come from General Talic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was my order. Tasks to the commanders of subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was a briefing by my subordinate units, their commanders, that is, and after this briefing, I issued tasks and assignments to those commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Would you go now to the 4th of June, then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we look at the report of Colonel Tepsic --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be at the level of the 1st Krajina Corps command, would it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He reported at the meeting with General Djukic about rear supplies for the corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what he reports there under paragraph 7, which comes right after 9 and before 4, "material reserves exhausted, no ammunition, spare parts, food."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it looks like the supply situation is worsening rather than improving?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because in point 9 of his report, he had informed that there were over 100.000 men in the corps. So the problem was how to ensure supplies for them all. That was four regular corps in strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was just virtually impossible to supply them with ammunition and food and things like that because it just wasn't available; fair statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and large consumption, particularly of fuel, ammunition, vehicles were used a lot and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you for letting me take so much of your time. I appreciate your efforts to answer my questions. And that's all I have for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Colonel, there is going to be a short re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour keeps saying short. I don't think I said short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's going to be about an hour. There is quite a lot I have to cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's going to take an hour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What about the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I'm about to raise with you. Mr. Nicholls has brought to my attention that she's been waiting in the witness room now for an hour, and if I finished at 5.30, I don't know how long Your Honours are going to be in asking questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be very few questions. Very few questions. A question of a couple of minutes. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, think we might start her then at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: We will require testing with the witness, 30 minutes I'm informed now, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean it can't be done outside court with the witness at present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. They require the witness sitting where Colonel Selak is sitting and test the equipment, et cetera. So basically we should --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It would have been nice if somebody told us that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I tried to avert previously, but I was told that doing what I suggested meant the technical staff not having a break and therefore, that is perfectly understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
