utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say, I think when Your Honour hears from the witness, I think Your Honour will accede to closed session rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe, maybe, maybe. Maybe what the situation as it is now, Ms. Korner, is that we will need to break at 5.15 in any case, and that's less than the hour that you require.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do need to break at 5.15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we break at 5.15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But we only started at 5 past 4.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an hour and a half any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyhow, Your Honour -- all that I'm asking Your Honour is to make a decision. Is this witness going to start this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are here at your disposal, Ms. Korner. I mean, there's no question about that. So -- but let's see how long your re-examination is going to take. Then perhaps halfway through or at some point in time, you yourself make a reassessment of the situation, keeping in mind that the technicians require a 30-minute break in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, it seems to me it's hardly worth it. Because all that would happen if Your Honour -- rather than seeing first whether you're going to grant closed session is going to have the half hour testing with the technicians just in case, and then there's no point, you can't start. In that case, Your Honour, she can't -- Your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Honour, I'm going to have to ask to call Mr. Mayhew first on Monday. He has to leave, finish his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's no problem -- that's no problem with us, but you understand, I'm sure you understand that we are dealing with a witness that has given evidence before, on previous occasions. It's true that you have explained to us that there are new circumstances that have come up, that would warrant a closed session, but honestly I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, in that case, it seems to me that the only solution is that if it requires half an hour's testing, that should happen when we finish with Colonel Selak and clearly the witness can't start until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason is that if we are satisfied that with these extra precautions, voice distortion or image distortion, he or she, so that we don't give an indication, would be sufficiently protected in addition to the precautionary protective measures that are already decided upon. We will go that way rather than go into closed session obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honour, I don't think it's -- but I can say if Your Honours minded to do that, the Court will be in and out of private session because the nature of the evidence is such that it identifies her. Anyhow, Your Honour, having said that, perhaps I can now continue with Colonel Selak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I know you've spent a very long time testifying. If you can just answer the questions directly that I ask - if I want more details I'll follow up - I think we get through it and let you go a little bit quicker. I want to deal first of all with the very last thing you were asked about virtually, and that is the attendance of General Talic at Crisis Staff meetings. And you've told us that in relation to the 18th of May, he didn't say directly that he'd just come from it, but from the very context and what he was saying, you took it he had been at the meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us earlier that though he personally wouldn't tell you that he had been to a Crisis Staff meeting, it was necessary that other officers were aware of his whereabouts at any given time. I want you to think back quite carefully. Were you told by other officers that General Talic when not at the post wherever he should have been, was attending a Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not told.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So how did you know that General Talic attended meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting with General Talic, I felt from what he said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Don't worry about the 18th of May. I think you've explained why. But at any other stage, are you saying that you knew or were told that General Talic was attending meetings of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed amongst ourselves, that is to say the officers, of the corps command, about these meetings. I never asked who attended them, whether Talic or one of his associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right. Now, before I move on, there is one matter that I just want -- if I could, Mr. Ackerman, to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that the suggestion that was put to the colonel yesterday that, when I asked in fact in terms, that Mr. Brdjanin never wore any kind of uniform, is not in fact the suggestion that Mr. Ackerman intended to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm authorised to say this: It was the representation I intended to make but it was my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I could notice I was looking at your client at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was told -- and my client has authorised me to tell you this, I was told by my client that what he said was not true because he didn't even have a uniform. And I concluded from that that meant he never wore one, and that's why I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Korner? I think that clears the situation?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back, please, briefly over a couple of matters that you were asked about yesterday. First of all, you were asked about Milan Martic and the fact that it wouldn't be unusual for a TO officer or whatever to be leading troops. I want you to look, please, and this is the last time --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, to correct it, the question had to do with the fact that he was the head of MUP and that MUP has police troops and that's -- it wasn't the head of TO. It had to do with his police position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the colonel had explained to you that he saw nothing strange in it in considering that he was a retired army officer or a reserve --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It was put to him that it would be -- the colonel said it would be logical -- at page 71 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For a professional soldier to stand at the head of an unit. However, if Mr. Martic was a reserve officer, then I see no reason why he shouldn't command an unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you -- and this is the last time, Colonel, I'm going to ask you to do this -- to look at your diary -- sorry, your official notebook, for April the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which Your Honours will find in the translation at page 104.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's headed, Colonel, "Jajce."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you record there something about a group hijacking vans, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you go on to say, "The group were Martic's men, who went about ill treating people"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that the same Martic that we are talking about? Or that Mr. Ackerman was asking you about, the Milan Martic, the minister in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, and from this report, were his men proper, authorised soldiers? Or police officers serving under a proper military command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Martic did not have his units in the Jajce area, Kljuc, Jajce, and Mrkonjic. This group of men, according to the report by the depot commander in Jajce arrived in a van, they took the van -- actually, how they came, that doesn't say, but he said they were Martic's men. I didn't ask him where he got this information from, how he knew they were Martic's men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From your own knowledge of that area, was that the only occasion that these so-called "Martic's men" committed criminal offences? Not just in Jajce but in other places.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we speak of the concept of Martic's men, in Banja Luka there was information along those lines, and people feared the very name of Martic's men when they heard it, because there were problems in my area of responsibility, which was Donji Vakuf, Jajce, and Mrkonjic, there were not any other cases except for this one but the word "Martic's men" would instill fear in us. It wasn't pleasant for us to hear it mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, next I want to deal with one of the documents that you were asked about again yesterday, and this in fact was P229, which is this document prepared or conclusions of a meeting of various municipalities, and I would like you now please -- and it was put to you that you don't know whether this document was actually ever sent to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the 1st Krajina Corps and you said no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you standing up for any reason, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm trying to find a book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you now please have a look at a document called -- with a number P247? And if we could have -- if it's possible to have the English, just the first page of the English, placed on the ELMO? Yes, thank you. Now, this is a document dated seven days later, the 14th of June. It's headed, instead of Sanski Most, "Intermunicipal agreement Sanska Unska area," but it's the same group of municipalities, it appears, Krupa, Petrovac, Novi, Dubica, Prijedor, and Sanski Most. And could you look at the last page, Colonel? Is that again the same stamp that we looked at last time but a rather fuller version?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, could you give me the -- and I'll find it for the colonel. Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the same stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is I think you told us the SDS party Sanski Most; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you just go to the first page --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, does that say, "With regard to the previous meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, we can note that most of our proposals have been adopted and have been incorporated into the official positions of the Crisis Staff taken at its 8th June, 1992 session." Now, we haven't got the record of that session, but we do have a radio announcement in relation to it. Could you look now, please, at Exhibit P233? And to remind ourselves that the 9th of June -- sorry, the 7th of June document from this group had asked for a purging of Muslims and Croats from the Krajina Corps. This is Banja Luka Radio, the 9th of June, which states this: "The Crisis Staff of the Krajina autonomous region has issued an announcement in which the following is stated: Urgent differentiation along national lines is required within the officer corps of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then it goes on to deal with centres of security services. Now, Colonel, you were asked this yesterday about the earlier document. Have you any reason to believe that either of these two documents, that is of the 7th of June or the 14th of June, are forgeries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are authentic documents. I believe in them completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that topic that you were asked about yesterday. Now, finally on yesterday's cross-examination, it was suggested to you, in no uncertain terms, that you were acting as a spy when you passed information to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in respect of what you learned of troop movements and the like. Whom did you regard as the legitimate government within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legitimate government in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- there was a referendum and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was officially proclaimed. It was recognised by the United Nations. And that was what I considered to be the legitimate government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for a legal opinion in any way, Colonel, but did you regard the so-called Serbian Republic of -- in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a legitimate government?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not consider it to be a legitimate government because it was proclaimed only by one nation, one ethnic group, whereas Bosnia-Herzegovina is a multi-ethnic state with three nationalities, Serbs, Bosniaks, and Muslims. And this was proclaimed by the Assembly of the Serbian People and for me, it was not legitimate, unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want now, then, please, to go back to questions you were asked during the first day you were cross-examined, I think the Tuesday of this week. And I want to deal with three different matters, please. First of all, you said to Mr. Ackerman, when he was asking you -- I will just find the page. Yes. He was asking you in respect of arming, and I'm going to come back to the two major documents but you said this: "In the Tribunal, there is a document from the commander of the 6th TO Brigade, Colonel Basara, October 1991." And then you explained you had an a copy of the document in which he explains emphatically and clearly how he armed the Serb people in Bosnian Krajina, Kljuc, and Sanski Most. That's at page 13.228 of the transcript. I'd like you to have a look now please at Exhibit P745. First, Colonel, is that the document you were thinking about? It may help if you look, please, under paragraph 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please. I haven't found it yet. One, two, three. I can't see number 4. Could you help me and read the text out?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it begins, "In the course of March, 1991, clashes between the nationalities intensified." I think you'll find it on page -- with the stamp number 00478674. Which begins with the word "Krajs" [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you go down that paragraph, and if the usher would be kind enough to put the English on to the ELMO so that everybody can see what we are looking at, do you see there, "We had to resort to a trick to make it possible for us to arm the Serbs publicly and legally"? And before that -- all right. Colonel, don't worry about that. Is this the --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All I want to know is: Did you know Colonel Basara?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, during the war, but I didn't know him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Would you be able to recognise his writing? Did you ever see his writing?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't be able to recognise his handwriting but I can see that this document speaks about what I quoted and what I noted down in my notebook. I quoted the document. I had it in my hands and I made a note of it and I'm reading from it, "We worked in two directions, the first to organise and arm the Serb people and the second to negotiate, persuading the Muslims and Croats to remain loyal." So that is the document. "In order to be able to arm the Serbs publicly, we had to resort to a trick to make it possible for us to arm the Serbs publicly and legally. The story was devised that the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps ordered" -- that's the document, but I don't know the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. That's all I ask from that document. You can put that away. Now, I want to deal with two allied topics. First of all, this question of those documents showing arms supplied by the 1st Krajina Corps. Could you have back, please, document 1572? Now, a lot of time was spent on this document, both when I asked you questions and when Mr. Ackerman did, but the situation as I understand your evidence now is that this relates to arms supplied to various TO staffs and units from 1991 onwards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And that was from the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And these arms could have been properly issued if these particular TO units had been actually mobilised?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in that case, the regular path would have been through the logistics base and not via the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It appears from the other documents you were shown by Mr. Ackerman, which showed a supply of arms to Kotor Varos that this may be an incomplete list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not everything is included here. I received an order to issue even machine-guns to the MUP units, the police units, so even a larger amount and a larger assortment of weapons and other equipment, everything that the units needed on the basis of their requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in order for them to be mobilised, as you and Mr. Ackerman -- or as you told Mr. Ackerman this morning, there had to be an order for mobilisation issued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There had been an order issued in September of 1991, in respect of the conflict in Croatia. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I too mobilised my logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, there are no dates on this so we don't know when these arms were issued. But can I just ask you this: Omarska, which is -- it's the tenth, I think, or ninth TO on this list, did that fall -- did that TO unit fall within any other area unit?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prijedor unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But it was issued separately with arms because we can see, I think, that Prijedor -- don't think -- a correction on this -- appears on this list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does Prijedor appear on this list?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor? I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So -- and can you just tell us this: Was Omarska a Serb ethnicity village or Muslim or mixed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure. I mean I'm sure it was mixed, but I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. don't know what the percentage was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to have again, please, the other document that you were asked about in respect of this, and that's 1573. Now, this is the one you were asked a lot of questions about, whether it was authorised or ordered or whatever. But the date is the 14th of March, 1992, and you've already told us that this particular village, Karanovac, was Serb.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Located five kilometres from Banja Luka, to the west, as you get out of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry about where it is.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vrbas canyon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do know the date of this. 14th of March, 1992. On the 14th of March, 1992, had any order for mobilisation been issued?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. That is, when it was issued in respect of individual units. I don't remember the date that there had been a mobilisation. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If there had not been, if evidence shows that there had been no mobilisation call, would there have been any reason for this village to have had this selection of weapons sent to it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my assessment, these weapons were issued to a 30 troop strong battalion for the purposes of controlling access roads to Banja Luka from the direction of Jajce and Mrkonjic Grad which were the only routes from the direction of Jajce along the Vrbas canyon towards Banja Luka. That is the only road that vehicles could take. It is a canyon that can be easily controlled with a battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But is that a -- that's -- you deduced that but was that is a legitimate reason for these -- for this village being given the weapons?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This does not seem to be logical to me because the small unit should have been part of a larger TO staff, a larger TO unit, such as a company or a battalion. To arm a small group of people, such as platoon, from the military point of view, doesn't seem logical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, was it the job, was it lawful, if you like, for a TO unit to, as you put it, control all the roads? Or was that a police job?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is in the spirit of the law, because normally, the civilian police is in charge of controlling the traffic, and the military police as well if necessary, in the area of combat operations, if there are no combat operations, then it is the job of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any combat operations going on on the 14th of March, around the area where this village was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not even throughout the war, there were no combat operations in this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Colonel. You can put that document away now. Now, you were asked this morning to look at the records of the TO units in Kozarac and to look at the weapons. I want you to have again, please, the document you looked at earlier, P1416. Now, you looked at it when I was asking you questions about the attack on Kozarac but this is for a different point. The motorised brigade that you described was supported by two 105-millimetre howitzer batteries and a tank squadron. Did any of the weapons that you looked at on the lists this morning compare with the type of weaponry that the VRS had?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for having smiled. The weapons that the so-called conditionally speaking Green Berets had and the weapons that this Motorised Brigade had, I mean, it's just toys compared to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What sort of weaponry would the VRS have had?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS had the most modern weapons, from the JNA, even a surplus of weapons that had been pulled out from Slovenia and Croatia and which were kept in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the JNA units, initially, later in the units of the VRS. As for automatic rifles -- correction, they had automatic rifles, all kinds of weapons, including M-84 tanks, MIG 21 and 25 aircraft, with complete logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Apart --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the assistance of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if the Prosecutor is now conceding that this document reflects an accurate account of what happened at Kozarac or -- in other words, does she accept paragraph 4 as well as paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's quite clear, that isn't even a question that deserves an answer. Your Honour, I'm asking the difference between what is put down here as what was engaged in the attack in Kozarac, I'm certainly not accepting, and Mr. Ackerman knows it, that to describe the total strength of the Green Berets as 1.500 to 2.000 men isn't in any way accurate and we've been through that. I'm merely comparing the relative strength of what's down here. But if Mr. Ackerman wants to suggest that they also lied about what they used I'm quite happy to take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the explanation forthcoming from Ms. Korner is a fair one, Mr. Ackerman. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, apart from the tanks and the weaponry, did the Motorised Brigade also have armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it had. In terms of formations, it is normal for a Motorised Brigade to have armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour said you wanted to have a break at 5.15. Perhaps I can just deal with one allied topic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked -- you were shown the -- the CSB version of what happened in Prijedor and Kozarac around this period of time, and you were asked whether you accepted that there was an attack on Prijedor, as was put in this report, launched by Muslims and Croatian extremists, 200 well armed and organised men launched an all-out attack on vital facilities and institutions. And you said you did not accept there was an attack on Prijedor. Now, I want you to have a look at another document on this, please. Could you look, please, at first of all, P937?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While they are looking for the document, how much longer do you expect your re-examination to last?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: About another 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have quite a lengthy section to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break. I think it's safer to have the break because we can run into the same problem we did last time when Mr. Trbojevic said he would only take 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was expecting to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the break but let's give the witness the document that -- the exhibit that you want to question him about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it can wait until after the break, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will do that after the break. Thank you. 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, this is a report -- one of the first KK reports, dated the 30th of May, and it deals under situation on the ground, with a description of what happened in Prijedor on the 29th, 30th of May. It says, "In the morning at about 0400 a group of Muslims extremists neutralised a position at the Sana River bridge, killing two sentries, overpowered the hotel Prijedor security guards." That's paragraph 3. "And using a Molotov cocktail, set fire to the hotel where the military police was accommodated." And then, "sniper fire in the vicinity of the hotel." And then, "eight extremists from the area of Donji Puharska opened fire on targets in the barracks. Heavy fighting is taking place in the town of Prijedor. The assault was carried out by a group of about 80 Muslim extremists." If you look, please, at the combat report for the next day, or the day after, that's Exhibit P655, that shows, under, "Situation in the units," "the 1st Krajina Corps in the areas of Prijedor, Kljuc, Sanski Most, et cetera, are in control of the situation and are continuing the mopping up." And so on and so forth. Now, do you remember that incident, when approximately 80 people, 80 Muslims, extremists or not, did try and seize part of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember this. I think that it would have been a suicide to attack the town of Prijedor, where a very powerful brigade, with almost 6.000 troops, was located. It is possible that there were individual actions, but that there was -- that there would have been an organised attack on the town, no, that would have been a suicide, as I said. I am not aware of this attack. I believe I already indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Colonel. Then I needn't trouble you further on that matter. Then the final top take I want to cover with you is this question of cooperation, military, political, and the exact meaning of orders. Now, Mr. Ackerman asked you a number of questions, and ended by showing you this document from Bosanska Krupa, which purports to give actual military orders to the units that were stationed there. Now, I want you to look, please, at a series of documents from different municipalities, at the end ask you to really sum up for us the nature of this type of cooperation. Can we start, please, by you having for a moment the gazettes, the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, P227? And could you go, please, to number 9?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is the 13th of May meeting. Paragraph 7, "The persons authorised to resolve all military and political --"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I have the 14th of May on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I -- it's -- you need to go to the 9th, as it were, meeting. It's the one of the 13th of May, and you'll find it on page --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. "The persons authorised to resolve all military and political issues in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are Vojo Kupresanin" --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you give me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Usher, just give me them?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it. Item 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And you see that, "The persons authorised to resolve all military and political issues in the autonomous region are Kupresanin and Radic." Now, can you go, please, to the meeting 11, which is the 15th of May?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of May, conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 5: "Talks should be held with General Talic about calling up and assigning military conscripts on the 20th and 21st of May, 1992." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've looked already at the 18th of May in respect of Kozmos and finally on these gazettes could you go to number 15, which is the 22nd of May meeting? Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th? Yes. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'll find -- I think you'll find that on --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'll find that on the page that's got the ERN number 00497848.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, conclusion 4, "In view of the presents poor coordination between the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the newly established army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, mandatory attendance of General Talic or a person designated by him is requested at the meetings of the Crisis Staff." 5, "The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina hereby demands that the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its ministry of the army urgently secure a passage, a corridor, to Semberija and Serbia in order to facilitate a flow of goods and people." Now, Colonel, do these sections represent the sort of cooperation and, if you put it that way, requests that were going on at the level of the ARK Regional Crisis Staff and the corps command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, it is the coordination in terms of tasks between the military and the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look, please, at some documents from various municipalities, and then ask you at the end the question. First, could you be given Exhibit P902?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This comes from the Kljuc municipality, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A letter from General Talic to the Kljuc Municipal Assembly, and also to the autonomous region assembly, 8th of May. "Dear sir," it reads, "you are well aware of the efforts we are investing together with you and the municipal leaderships in preserving the peace in Krajina. We would have failed in these efforts had it not been for the high level of cooperation between the military and civilian authorities which we have no doubt shall continue." And then, it goes on to say, "We are dissatisfied with the cooperation provided by the municipal organs in Kljuc." And then it goes on to describe Chetnik units, "units being encouraged to dessert under the pretext they are going to defend Kljuc. Two Muslims killed for unknown reasons and the president of the municipal assembly is attempting to exercise command over the JNA units in the area." And it goes on to ask for the intercession of various people. Next, please, could you look at again, it's P208. Dealing with this in order. This is Sanski Most Crisis Staff meeting, 27th of May, 1992 -- I'm sorry, Kljuc, sorry, again. Item number 10. "The relationship of the military authorities to the civilian authorities should be such that the military will execute the orders of the civilian authorities while the civilian authorities will not interfere with the way these orders are carried out." And I'll come back to that at the end. Next could you be shown, please -- now this is a document that doesn't have an exhibit number yet, it's disclosure number is 3.202, and we have copies available for Their Honours, the Registry, and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, may that then be marked P1607 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1067"]?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this comes from Kotor Varos, 24th of June, 1992, Crisis Staff meeting. Item number 3: "After a discussion of the work of the security station, it was concluded that the Crisis Staff has no right to interfere in the professional work of the police and army, and that no one wishes or requires it to take upon itself security --"

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I do not have that document. This is from the 36th session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Yes. Can you look at item 3?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does it start, "Inspector Pejic"?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. On this date, the 24th of June, the Crisis Staff is saying that it shouldn't interfere in the professional work of the army. Next, please, I'd like you to have a look at another document from Kotor Varos, and that's 3.223, which will become Exhibit 1608. And I'll hand those out as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 65, line 21, is should be, I think, 1607, not 1067.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite possible I said that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you didn't. No, you definitely said 1607.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the other thing is at 66, line 9, Ms. Korner says that this document says that the Crisis Staff is saying that it shouldn't interfere in the professional work of the army and that's -- that is a misquote, because what it says is that it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I read out the exact quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That it has no right to interfere, not that it shouldn't but that it has no right to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I read out the exact quote earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct and I have the impression that she did read out has no right, in fact, because I remember it vividly. Okay. But in any case, thank you, Mr. Ackerman, for pointing that out, and you, Ms. Korner, for confirming it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could the witness look at the next one which is the 14th of July, Kotor Varos again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item 1, "Mane Tepic and Savo Tepic briefly expanded Presidency members on combat operations. Based on this information, the War Presidency concluded it was not satisfied with the results achieved so far and the current military and security situation. It was further concluded that General Talic and Stojan Zupljanin chief of the CSB have to be contacted urgently in order to inform them of our satisfaction of development so far and task them with creating conditions needed to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accelerate late the operation." All right. Next please, I'm sorry, there are only another three documents. Could you be handed Exhibit 7 -- P710?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This last document, was it given an exhibit number, 3223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1608, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is the Sanski Most municipal assembly on the 27th of July, because then it had gone back to an assembly. Can you turn, please, Colonel, to item number 4?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 27th of July, I hope.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 4, when the chairman opened the debate on the political and security situation. Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then this is rather difficult but can you -- if you move down the paragraph, just before a man called Boro Savanovic speaks, you should find a sentence reading as follows: "The command of the 6th Krajina Brigade should be relocated to Sanski Most and the chairman of the executive committee should put this forward at a meeting of the government of the autonomous - it reads republic, but it must be - region of Krajina. So there they were saying this is what they wanted to happen and they would put it forward. Now, could you look, please, at document P746? Which is a description generally of the work of the 6th Krajina Brigade. If you turn, please, Colonel, in that -- I'm afraid this is rather difficult. It's a paragraph, a short paragraph, that begins, "On the 28th of August."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's at our page 9, Your Honours, and it's just above a list of brigade commanding officers.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found that yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You will find that, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, page 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But that's the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1992, the command of the brigade with headquarters support units relocated from Lusci Palanka to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is about -- almost exactly a month after that last request. Now, finally on this topic could you be shown P733 and P735.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basara.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 733, please, first of all. Sanski Most again, November, 1992 now.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item 2, "Arrange a visit to the 1st Krajina Corps command, inform the corps commander of the situation in the municipality. The issue of reducing the number of battalions in the 6th Krajina Brigade to four. Respect of the army command for work obligation. The issue of course is for military officers," and so on and then the delegation. And then item number 4, "The 6th Krajina Brigade command is asked to analyse its work and make personnel changes." Thank you. That's all I want on that document. And the final document I want now, I assure you, Colonel, is Exhibit P735. 17th of November, 1992, Sanski Most again. "The command of the 6th Krajina Brigade and the public security station are requested to submit a report on who participated in the organisation of the armed attack on Trnovo and Sehovci and what was the goal of an attack on such a scale? The perpetrators of this horrible crime must be urgently found and the most severe measures provided by the law taken against them. The 6th Krajina Brigade and the public security station are hereby requested to provide security for all citizens of Sanski Most municipality and their property." All right. Colonel, that's it. Thank you. I'm sorry to have taken so long with the documents. Now, Mr. Ackerman, in a rather dramatic way, suggested that the way that Krupa attempted to give orders to the military was laughable. I think he said, "When they stopped laughing." Having looked at all these documents and from your own knowledge, although the civilian, political authorities could not give orders in the military sense to the military, order them to do things, could they, as we've seen, have an influence on what the military actually did by making these requests, and in some case dressing them up as orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object for a couple of reasons. First of all, he's already answered that question twice at least in the course of his testimony. He has said that a civilian authority could at any time could make requests of the military and the military could decide what they wanted to do about that request. Either passing it up the chain of command or within the authority of the local commander, go ahead and carry it out if he thought it was appropriate. That's in the record. It's been put in at least twice. I asked both of us asked him about it. Second of all, it seems to me it's rather unfair to go through this whole list of documents and not ask him a question along this line about the document while he's looking at it, and ask him to try to give some kind of a summary answer after having looked at all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You did exactly the same thing yesterday for almost an hour, Mr. Ackerman. And I'm allowing the question for a very simple reason: That in the course of your cross-examination, you showed the witness other documents purporting to prove exactly the opposite of what is being suggested now by Ms. Korner. So particularly -- particularly with reference to Krupa, which is specifically being referred to by Ms. Korner in the beginning of her question. And that arises precisely from your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there may be a misunderstanding because that was a document where a civilian leader actually issued a document that was called an order, purporting to order the military to do something. All these document that is Ms. Korner has been going through this afternoon all say requesting the military to do things and the that the military should do certain things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not actually right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Your objection is not being sustained, Mr. Ackerman. And Ms. Korner,

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, all I want to know is: Looking at these documents and from your own knowledge is it as simple a concept as Mr. Ackerman would have it, that the military only carry out its own orders without effectively any input into those orders from the political?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is absolutely not my position. I went through the whole thing that the military is under the control of the civilian Commander-in-Chief, and of course they do everything under their control. And I never said what she suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. In a way you didn't say, because what you suggested in the course of your cross-examination was as follows: That the military authorities took orders from the higher echelons of the military organisation itself, except in as far as the President of the republic with specific reference to Mr. Karadzic at the time that you mentioned, and previously the relative political -- the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As the chief of -- Commander-in-Chief, as the Commander-in-Chief, that was your suggestion. But the witness did also, as a result of several questions that you put to him, and some documents that you should to him, tend to suggest that there were instances where the military would not be subjected to any kind of interference or influence on the part of the civilian authorities. And what Ms. Korner is precisely asking of the witness is to clarify this position on the basis of the documents that she has shown him now. This is why I'm telling you that her question is perfectly in order and I'm allowing it. Perhaps you may prefer to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the suggestion as I understand it from Mr. Ackerman was that effectively the only political authority that could have any control or influence over what the army did was the Commander-in-Chief, the very top level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's absolutely not the case. My question had to do with chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Superior-subordinate relationships. The superior-subordinate relations go through the army chain of command from the Commander-in-Chief now. No intervening civilian authority has a superior relationship over any army unit. Those are exactly the questions I asked and exactly the answers I got.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not suggesting for one movement, and that's not what my question about. But the impression was clearly left by Mr. Ackerman that effectively it was laughable for any municipality president or authority or regional to attempt to, as it were, get the army to do things. I am merely asking Colonel Selak if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. That is not what I said. I said it was laughable for somebody to order the army to do something. Not to try to get them to do it. He said, and I have said all along, that the army can request all they want to. I mean, the civilians can request all they want to and then the army decides what they are going to do about it, but this document was an order. He was purporting to order the army to do something. And the witness correctly said to me, no he can't do that. He can't order the army to do something. That's the issue. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct with regard to that Krupa incident. But as regards the rest, the question that Ms. Korner has put is perfectly legitimate and it is arising out of the cross-examination. So I am allowing the question. And, Colonel, please -- I would suggest that you repeat the question because now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I can't remember what it is either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, having looked at all these documents and from your own knowledge, the relationship below the republic Commander-in-Chief, a simple -- that the municipality and the regional level couldn't issue orders, and that was the end of that, or was this a more complex relationship?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship was a little more complex. To order the use of units by the municipal authorities is something that could not have taken place. However, in certain cases, and in some of the previous documents, where investigations were called for with respect to certain sabotage activity or the killing of certain persons, et cetera, the army had to be involved, and engaged, because it was assumed that some of the perpetrators may have been army members. So they had this common goal, and the municipal authorities and the units located in the area had to cooperate in matters of this kind. So let me repeat. The head of the municipality could not issue orders to the brigade commander to have the brigade deployed. However, in the area of responsibility where there were common problems, they had to discuss things and reach agreements as to what was to be done. Have I been clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you finally, Colonel, and this is the last question: Does the part that I read from the document -- yes, the -- it was Exhibit P208, from Kljuc, where they say, "The relationship of the military authorities to the civilian authorities should be such that the military will execute the orders of the civilian authorities while the civilian authorities will not interfere with the way those orders are carried out." Does that seem an accurate summary of the relationship?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorisation has been overstepped by the President of the Crisis Staff. He has overstepped his authority to command, issue commands and orders to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But if the situation is this: The political authorities say, "This from a political point of view is what needs doing, we, the political authorities tell the army this is what needs doing but you do it in the way you think proper." Is that a fair summary of what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is being misquoted again by Ms. Korner. The document says, and she quoted it right above, from Kljuc, says, "The relationship of the military authorities to the civilian authorities should be such that the military will do this." Not that it is. This is a wish, and the wish was never granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken. But I don't think she is misquoting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I quoted exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She did read out the text verbatim and I don't think the colonel did not understand the question. I'm not quite sure whether he is directing his answer bull's eye where it should be, but put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think and certainly I think the colonel and everybody else in this Court is quite tired on a Friday afternoon let me just try one more time a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yesterday, or the day before, when Mr. Ackerman and earlier, when you were testifying, you explained that it was the political who set the goals. They were then carried out by the military. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The actual orders to the military could only come from the political Commander-in-Chief, if you like, that is, as you pointed out, Mr. Karadzic, and the actual order to carry out an attack or deploy or whatever could only come within the military chain of command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But at the regional level or at the municipal level, in this cooperation that was going on, if the regional level said, "This is an objective that needs to be achieved," as we looked at now, or at the municipal level, and you the army should carry this out because it's within your sphere of competence, is that something that would carry weight, even if, as you say, they couldn't give an order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been asked and answered about ten times now, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just finishing off, thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Korner, and please bring it to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unit commander, if he had the authority and duty to carry something out, he would have done so. Now, if this went against his authorisations and competence and assignments, he would not carry it out. However, he would have to inform his superior of the problem that had arisen between the civilian organs of power and authority and his own particular unit, and likewise, the civilian authority would have to follow its own hierarchy and chain to solve the problem. However, there were very few such problems in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that was why?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the goal was the same: The creation of a state called Republika Srpska. And the goal uses all the means it can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Colonel Selak. That really is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had one re-cross question with regard to Exhibit P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the question is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was the contention of the Prosecutor, or suggested by the Prosecutor, that General Talic had attended the Crisis Staff meeting of the 18th of May. And document P227, I just would like to ask the witness if it's not a bit strange that four days later they would be demanding his presence at the Crisis Staff contending that he had never attends, if he'd been there four days before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not even a proper question on any showing and it's one that could have been asked a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could have been asked and I think the position has been made quite clear by the witness. I mean why he concluded -- he reached the conclusion that he reached. I don't think it's going to change anything basically. Yes, Judge Janu. I believe you have some questions. Go ahead. Colonel, we have some questions from the bench

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Colonel Selak, I have two simple questions for you. I would like to go back to your statement, first one, from the year 1995-96, and you stated there that the top three reasons for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina were, first, Serb nationalism; second, the propaganda of Orthodox Church; and the third one, propaganda of Serbian academy of art and science. My question is: I would like limited myself to the second and third point, because on the first one, we already have heard quite a lot of -- we have quite a lot of evidence. So I'm interested in the propaganda of the Orthodox Church and propaganda of Serbian academy of science. My question is: Who was involved in this propaganda, concerning the Orthodox Church. Was it just individuals from the structure of the church or was it the top leadership, top clergy? And if you can provide Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us with some names, I would be happy about that. And in the Serbian academy of science, the same, if it was the top or just individuals in the structure, and if you know some names, please give it to us. That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel. And please try to be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media reported on this, in Serbia, for instance, that the objective of creating a Greater Serbia, a meeting was held at the Belgrade patriarchy, attended by the federal secretariat for National Defence, General Adzic, patriarch German. I don't know who represented the academy of science. It was mentioned in the conclusions that, with the purpose of creating a Greater Serbia, we are prepared to sacrifice as many as 70.000 lives. There is a document to that effect in Serbia. Therefore, the Orthodox Church was also in favour of Greater Serbia. And the history has taught us that as early as during the Balkan wars, this was the case. I don't know whether I've been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And my second question is going back to the meeting from your official notebook, and you don't need the document. It was the meeting with the directors of Rudi Cajavec and Kozmos, and there were present directors and there were also present two generals, General Dukic and General Nikitovic, and I don't know, Major Tepsic and others. And the discussion was going on and concerning the -- for example, production of ammunition. There was a problem of the defined status of military industry firm. I think this meeting was in connection how to convert these companies to the military sphere, for ammunition, and there were of course because the war wasn't declared there were some problems. I understood this document this way. And there was also present Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Radic, president of the municipality. And Mr. Brdjanin in this connection, when, among all these technical problems of conversion, for example to invite the experts from Federal Republic of Serbia, to help with this, Mr. Brdjanin stated, "the production must begin as soon as possible." And the statement of President Radic was something like, something similar. He said, "If we go to the government, it will be too slow, so it must be organised on the municipal level and there shouldn't be any delays because of the administration." My question is: Could a person without power and authority make such a request in the presence of representative of the army, I mean statement of Mr. Brdjanin. That's one part of the question. A second one is: What was the reaction of the military officials to this request?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rudi Cajavec factory belonged to the municipality, to the town of Banja Luka, and it also manufactured some military equipment. It needed to be reorganised in order to be able to manufacture ammunition as well, and experts were being sought for that purpose. President Radic wanted to speed up this process, and he suggested that the government should be bypassed in order not to waste time. That is at least how I understood him. General Djukic was also in favour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not answering the question, Colonel. The question was this: With reference to what Mr. Brdjanin allegedly said in the course of that meeting, according to you, could a person without power and authority make such a request in the presence of representatives of the army? That's question number one. Your answer, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Next question: What was the reaction of the military officials to this request?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't react at all, and it was decided that they should start with the production as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's it. Okay, Colonel, I'm sorry to have been so abrupt with you at this very last part of the sitting. I know that everyone is tired. I thank you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, just a few words. Honourable Judges, I wish to inform you that, as a 6-year-old boy in 1941, at the beginning of the Second World War, I was placed in a children's home where I spent almost 15 years. I was educated and brought up by the state. In this home, in this orphan age, we socialised according to our inclinations and not in accordance to our religious or ethnic affiliations. And it was to this multi-ethnic state and multi-ethnic army that I gave my oath of loyalty. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there are many people now with the same beliefs, who hold the same beliefs as I do. We are sparing no effort to have -- in order to create once again a new Bosnia and Herzegovina, a prosperous country for all its citizens and all its three constituent peoples who must people at home in this state. Your Honours, your assistance and your help is invaluable for us in our efforts, and I should like to express my sincere gratitude to you. Thank you very much for allowing me to say these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. On our part, on behalf of the Tribunal and this Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over and give evidence. I know that this must have been quite tiring for you. You've been here for more than a week. This has now come to an end. Once more, I thank you. You will be assisted by the officers of this Tribunal to arrange for your return trip home, and on our part, we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you. Ms. Korner, Monday, Mr. Mayhew first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Mayhew and then the witness who had been here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to offer DB116 through DB128.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. They are so admitted and yours too. That's the end. Thank you. Have a nice weekend.
